stories.headline: FED HOLDS AT 3.75%-4.00% IN 10-2 SPLIT VOTE AS WARSH FACES DOUBLE DISSENT FOR A HIKE
stories.body: The FOMC left its target range unchanged at 3.75%-4.00% Wednesday, with Governor Lisa Cook and Cleveland Fed President Beth Hammack both dissenting in favor of a 25-basis-point hike. The S&P 500 added 0.30% to 7,743.98 and the Nasdaq rose on the hold, even as futures markets now price roughly an 84% chance of a hike at the December meeting.
stories.explain: A dissent is a formal, recorded vote against the majority — rare enough that two in one meeting is itself a signal, telling markets that at least a sixth of the committee sees current policy as too loose given inflation the statement itself called 'elevated.' Fed funds futures don't reprice off the vote count directly; they reprice off what that count implies about the distribution of views inside the room, which is exactly why December hike odds jumped even though nothing in the actual rate changed today.

stories.headline: OIL SPIKES ON UNCONFIRMED HOUTHI STRIKE CLAIM AGAINST SAUDI'S RAS TANURA REFINERY
stories.body: WTI crude jumped 2.9% to settle at $102.78 a barrel and Brent rose 1.3% to $115.32 after a reported Houthi missile claim against Saudi Arabia's Ras Tanura export terminal, testing the de-escalation discount that had built up since Monday's Tehran talks. Riyadh has not confirmed any damage, so traders are pricing headline risk, not a verified supply loss.
stories.explain: Oil's price has two parts: a fundamental supply-demand level and a geopolitical risk premium added or stripped out purely on the probability that a disruption actually removes barrels from the market. Ras Tanura is one of the world's largest export terminals, so even an unconfirmed claim against it forces traders to price in the tail risk before Saudi officials can verify or deny it — which is why the move happened within hours of the claim, well ahead of any physical confirmation.

stories.headline: 10-YEAR YIELD TOPS 5% AGAIN AS TERM PREMIUM OUTRUNS THE FED'S HOLD
stories.body: The 10-year Treasury yield climbed roughly 3 basis points to about 5.02% even as the Fed stood pat, extending a months-long rise that has little to do with the fed funds rate itself. Rising oil prices, a still-ballooning federal deficit, and heavy AI-capex-driven corporate borrowing are all competing for the same pool of long-duration capital.
stories.explain: The Fed sets the overnight rate; the 10-year is a market price built from the average expected path of that rate over a decade, plus a term premium investors demand for the risk of being wrong about inflation or deficits over that horizon. Today's move came almost entirely from the term-premium side — the same dynamic behind 1994's 'bond massacre' — which is why a Fed that just held steady can still watch its most important long-end benchmark climb against it.

stories.headline: GOLD SLIPS TO $4,035 AS DOLLAR FIRMS AND OIL ABSORBS THE SAFE-HAVEN BID
stories.body: Spot gold fell about 0.6% to $4,035.48 an ounce as the dollar index firmed roughly 0.1% to 102.42, with today's geopolitical premium flowing almost entirely into crude rather than bullion.
stories.explain: Gold and oil both carry crisis premiums, but they respond to different triggers — gold mainly to currency and real-rate moves, oil to physical supply threats. When a headline specifically threatens tanker traffic or a refinery, as today's Ras Tanura claim did, capital chases the asset with the most direct exposure, leaving gold exposed to the more mundane headwind of a modestly stronger dollar instead of catching a safe-haven bid of its own.

stories.headline: HOUSTON'S ROSTER EXODUS AND KANSAS'S NO. 1 RECRUIT HIGHLIGHT A REASSEMBLED PRESEASON TOP 25
stories.body: Florida enters the season as the preseason AP No. 1 for the first time since 2006, with Duke second and Illinois third, but the more disruptive stories sit lower down: preseason No. 10 Houston lost four key rotation pieces — Kingston Flemings, Chris Cenac Jr., Emanuel Sharp and Milos Uzan — while Kansas added five-star freshman Tyran Stokes, ESPN's No. 1 overall prospect in the class.

stories.headline: THUNDER'S TITLE DEFENSE ROCKED BY JALEN WILLIAMS, CASON WALLACE SURGERIES
stories.body: Oklahoma City will be without Jalen Williams (fractured fibula, dislocated ankle) and Cason Wallace (torn labrum) for extended stretches after GM Sam Presti confirmed surgery for each; Alex Caruso also left Monday's 125-114 win over Phoenix early with a right ankle sprain. The injury wave already has the defending champs fielding trade calls on depth guards like Ty Jerome.

stories.headline: SEAHAWKS LAND ALL-PRO GUARD QUENTON NELSON IN TRADE WITH COLTS
stories.body: Seattle acquired six-time All-Pro guard Quenton Nelson from Indianapolis for a 2027 third-round pick and a 2028 fifth, waiving incumbent guard Christian Haynes to make room. The 4-3 Seahawks remain in the running for Colts RB Jonathan Taylor too, though the Nelson deal leaves them with less draft capital to meet Indianapolis's reported asking price.

stories.headline: WASHINGTON'S QB SITUATION STAYS UNRESOLVED DAYS BEFORE FIRST-EVER TRIP TO NEBRASKA
stories.body: Huskies coach Jedd Fisch again declined to name a starter between Demond Williams Jr., working back from the fractured rib he suffered Oct. 9 against Iowa, and Elijah Brown, who threw three interceptions but still rallied Washington past Purdue 38-26 in relief. Nebraska, 5-2 and 2-2 in Big Ten play, hosts Saturday's first-ever conference meeting between the two programs.

sports.detail: 4-3 after acquiring All-Pro guard Quenton Nelson from the Colts for a 2027 third and 2028 fifth-round pick. Seattle is still chasing a Jonathan Taylor deal but has less draft capital to spend; hosts Chicago on Monday Night Football.

deepDive.title: Reading an FOMC Dissent: Why Two 'No' Votes Pushed December Hike Odds to 84%
content: Today's Fed decision looked, on the surface, like a non-event: the committee held its target range at 3.75%-4.00%, exactly what markets expected. But the vote wasn't unanimous — Governor Lisa Cook and Cleveland Fed President Beth Hammack both dissented in favor of a 25-basis-point hike, the first double dissent of Chair Kevin Warsh's tenure. That detail matters more than the headline decision, arriving the same day oil spiked on an unconfirmed Middle East attack claim and the 10-year yield pushed back above 5%. A split vote in that backdrop isn't noise — it's the clearest signal the Fed has given in months about how close the committee is to moving again.

The FOMC's 12 voting seats rotate among the seven Washington-based Governors, the New York Fed president (a permanent voter), and four of the remaining eleven Reserve Bank presidents on an annual rotation. A dissent is a formal, recorded break from the majority — rare by design, since the Fed values the appearance of consensus to keep its signal clean. When two voters break ranks in the same direction, it tells the market that the center of gravity inside the room has shifted further than the statement's own careful language — 'inflation remains elevated' — lets on. Markets don't trade the vote tally itself; they trade what the tally implies about the next six weeks of data the committee will be weighing.

The mechanism connecting a dissent to a futures price is indirect but real: CME FedWatch-style odds are built from fed funds futures contracts, which price in trader expectations for the rate at each future meeting. Those expectations move on every new data point, but a visible split at the top accelerates the repricing because it confirms, rather than merely suggests, that hawkish members are willing to act on the data rather than wait. The closest precedent is 1994's so-called 'bond market massacre,' when a telegraphed tightening cycle still produced outsized long-yield moves because investors kept revising how far the committee's internal consensus would ultimately travel. Dissents are one of the few moments that consensus becomes visible in real time.

For today's specific setup, the dissent lands on top of two other inflationary inputs: an oil price that just jumped nearly 3% on an unverified refinery-attack claim, and a 10-year yield that's been climbing for weeks on deficit and AI-capex borrowing pressure, independent of anything the Fed does. Put together, two hawkish dissents plus a fresh oil shock is why December hike odds sit near 84% rather than near zero, the way they would have looked a month ago. The lesson for watching the next six weeks: the number to track isn't just the next CPI print, it's whether oil's move today holds — because that's the input most likely to turn today's minority view into December's majority one.
